arXiv:1201.3587v2 [math.CO] 13 Nov 2012

Turán densities of hypercubes

Rahil Baber
August 24, 2026
Abstract

In this paper we describe a number of extensions to Razborov’s semidefinite flag algebra method. We will begin by showing how to apply the method to significantly improve the upper bounds of edge and vertex Turán density type results for hypercubes. We will then introduce an improvement to the method which can be applied in a more general setting, notably to 33-uniform hypergraphs, to get a new upper bound of 0.56150.5615 for π⁡(K43)\pi(K_{4}^{3}).

For hypercubes we improve Thomason and Wagner’s result on the upper bound of the edge Turán density of a 4-cycle free subcube to 0.603180.60318 and Chung’s result on forbidding 6-cycles to 0.365770.36577. We also show that the upper bound of the vertex Turán density of 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3} can be improved to 0.769000.76900, and that the vertex Turán density of 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3} with one vertex removed is precisely 2/32/3.

1 Introduction

Razborov’s flag algebra method introduced in [17] has proven to be an invaluable tool in finding upper bounds of Turán densities of hypergraphs. Many results have been found through its application, for some such results and descriptions of the semidefinite flag algebra method as applied to hypergraphs see [1], [5], [6], [12], [18]. Later in this paper we will describe how to improve the bounds Razborov’s method is able to attain, in particular by using partially defined graphs. However, to begin with we will extend Razborov’s method from hypergraphs to hypercubes.

An nn-dimensional hypercube 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} is a 22-graph with 2n2^{n} vertices. Setting V⁡(𝒬n)={0,1,…,2n−1}V(\mathcal{Q}_{n})=\{0,1,\ldots,2^{n}-1\} we can define E⁡(𝒬n)E(\mathcal{Q}_{n}) as follows: v1​v2∈E⁡(𝒬n)v_{1}v_{2}\in E(\mathcal{Q}_{n}) if and only if v1v_{1} differs from v2v_{2} by precisely one digit in their binary representations. For example E⁡(𝒬2)={01,02,13,23}E(\mathcal{Q}_{2})=\{01,02,13,23\} (see also Figure 1). It is easy to see that the binary representations of the vertices indicate the coordinates of the vertices of a unit hypercube in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Let us also define the layers of a hypercube which will be useful later. Layer mm of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} consists of all vertices in V⁡(𝒬n)V(\mathcal{Q}_{n}) which have mm digits that are one in their binary representations. For example in 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3}, layer 0={0}0=\{0\}, layer 1={1,2,4}1=\{1,2,4\}, layer 2={3,5,6}2=\{3,5,6\}, and layer 3={7}3=\{7\}, see Figure 1.

We will consider two different types of Turán problems involving hypercubes. In the first type we will be interested in the following question: given a forbidden family of graphs ℱ\mathcal{F}, what is the maximum number of edges an ℱ\mathcal{F}-free subgraph of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} can have? We are particularly interested in the limit of the maximum hypercube edge density as nn tends to infinity, where we define the hypercube edge density of a subgraph GG of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} to be |E⁡(G)|/|E⁡(𝒬n)||E(G)|/|E(\mathcal{Q}_{n})|. We will refer to the limit as the edge Turán density

πe(ℱ)=limn→∞maxG{|E(G)|/|E(𝒬n)|:G⊆𝒬n, and is ℱ-free},\pi_{e}(\mathcal{F})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\max_{G}\{|E(G)|/|E(\mathcal{Q}_{n})|:G\subseteq\mathcal{Q}_{n},\textrm{ and is $\mathcal{F}$-free}\},

a simple averaging argument shows it always exists.

Motivation to study the edge Turán density comes from Erdős [11] who conjectured that πe​(𝒬2)=1/2\pi_{e}(\mathcal{Q}_{2})=1/2. It is easily seen that πe​(𝒬2)≥1/2\pi_{e}(\mathcal{Q}_{2})\geq 1/2 by taking 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} and removing those edges that have one vertex in layer 2​r−12r-1 and the other in layer 2​r2r for each rr. Such subgraphs of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} are 𝒬2\mathcal{Q}_{2}-free and contain exactly half the edges. The densest known constructions which are 𝒬2\mathcal{Q}_{2}-free are given by Brass, Harborth, and Nienborg [9], and they have a hypercube edge density of approximately (1+1/n)/2(1+1/\sqrt{n})/2. Chung [10] showed that πe​(𝒬2)≤(2+13)/9=0.62284\pi_{e}(\mathcal{Q}_{2})\leq(2+\sqrt{13})/9=0.62284, her argument was extended by Thomason and Wagner [19] using a computer, to get the previously best known bound of 0.622560.62256. By extending Razborov’s semidefinite flag algebra technique to hypercubes we will prove a significantly smaller upper bound of 0.606800.60680. Later we will improve this bound further to 0.603180.60318 using partially defined hypercubes. Chung [10] also considered the edge Turán density of 66-cycles, and proved 1/4≤πe​(C6)≤2−1=0.414211/4\leq\pi_{e}(C_{6})\leq\sqrt{2}-1=0.41421. We will improve the upper bound to 0.375500.37550, then using partially defined hypercubes reduce it further to 0.365770.36577.

The second type of hypercube Turán problem we will look at is very similar to the first but focuses on the density of vertices rather than edges. In the second type we are interested in the following question: given a forbidden family of graphs ℱ\mathcal{F}, what is the maximum number of vertices an ℱ\mathcal{F}-free induced subgraph of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} can have? We are particularly interested in the limit of the maximum hypercube vertex density as nn tends to infinity, where we define the hypercube vertex density of an induced subgraph GG of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} to be |V⁡(G)|/|V⁡(𝒬n)||V(G)|/|V(\mathcal{Q}_{n})|. We will refer to the limit as the vertex Turán density

πv(ℱ)=limn→∞maxG{|V(G)|/|V(𝒬n)|:G is an ℱ-free induced subgraph of 𝒬n},\pi_{v}(\mathcal{F})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\max_{G}\{|V(G)|/|V(\mathcal{Q}_{n})|:\textrm{$G$ is an $\mathcal{F}$-free induced subgraph of $\mathcal{Q}_{n}$}\},

again a simple averaging argument shows it always exists.

The analogous problem to Erdős’ conjecture is calculating πv​(𝒬2)\pi_{v}(\mathcal{Q}_{2}). E.A. Kostochka [16] and independently Johnson and Entringer [15] showed that πv​(𝒬2)=2/3\pi_{v}(\mathcal{Q}_{2})=2/3. Johnson and Talbot [14] proved that πv​(R1)=2/3\pi_{v}(R_{1})=2/3, where R1R_{1} is the graph formed by removing vertices 00 and 11 from 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3}. By extending Razborov’s semidefinite flag algebra method we will prove πv​(R2)=2/3\pi_{v}(R_{2})=2/3, where R2R_{2} is the graph formed by removing a single vertex from 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3}. The value of πv​(𝒬3)\pi_{v}(\mathcal{Q}_{3}), however, still remains undetermined. A lower bound of 3/43/4 is easily achieved by considering the induced subgraphs of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} formed by removing all vertices in layers that are a multiple of four (i.e. layers 0,4,8,…0,4,8,\ldots). Although we could not show πv​(𝒬3)≤3/4\pi_{v}(\mathcal{Q}_{3})\leq 3/4 we will prove πv​(𝒬3)≤0.76900\pi_{v}(\mathcal{Q}_{3})\leq 0.76900. We will also show that 1/2≤πv​(C6)≤0.531111/2\leq\pi_{v}(C_{6})\leq 0.53111.

2 Vertex Turán density

Calculating the vertex Turán density involves looking at induced subgraphs of hypercubes. However, the structure of the hypercubes may not be retained by the induced subgraphs. This structure will prove to be useful and will simplify definitions later. Hence rather than work directly with induced subgraphs we will instead use vertex-coloured hypercubes that represent induced subgraphs of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n}. In particular we will colour the vertices red and blue. The induced subgraph that a red-blue vertex-coloured hypercube represents can be constructed by removing those vertices that are coloured red (as well as any edges that are incident to such vertices) and keeping those vertices that are blue. The conjecture that πv​(𝒬3)=3/4\pi_{v}(\mathcal{Q}_{3})=3/4 comes from asking what is the maximum number of vertices a 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3}-free induced subgraph of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} can have. It is clear that this is equivalent to asking what is the maximum number of blue vertices a vertex-coloured 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} can have such that it does not contain an all blue 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3}. Therefore the problem of calculating πv​(𝒬3)\pi_{v}(\mathcal{Q}_{3}), and πv​(ℱ)\pi_{v}(\mathcal{F}) in general, can be translated into a problem involving forbidding vertex-coloured hypercubes in a vertex-coloured 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n}. We will define the equivalent notion of vertex Turán density for vertex-coloured hypercubes shortly, but first we need some definitions.

We will use the notation (n,κ)v(n,\kappa)_{v} to represent a vertex-coloured 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n}, where κ:V⁡(𝒬n)→{red, blue}\kappa:V(\mathcal{Q}_{n})\to\{\text{red, blue}\}. We define V⁡(F)V(F) and E⁡(F)E(F) for a vertex-coloured hypercube F=(n,κ)vF=(n,\kappa)_{v} to be V⁡(𝒬n)V(\mathcal{Q}_{n}) and E⁡(𝒬n)E(\mathcal{Q}_{n}) respectively. Consider two vertex-coloured hypercubes F1=(n1,κ1)v,F_{1}=(n_{1},\kappa_{1})_{v}, and F2=(n2,κ2)vF_{2}=(n_{2},\kappa_{2})_{v}. We say F1F_{1} is isomorphic to F2F_{2} if there exists a bijection f:V⁡(F1)→V⁡(F2)f:V(F_{1})\to V(F_{2}) such that for all v1​v2∈E⁡(F1)v_{1}v_{2}\in E(F_{1}), f⁡(v1)​f​(v2)∈E⁡(F2)f(v_{1})f(v_{2})\in E(F_{2}) and for all v∈V⁡(F1)v\in V(F_{1}), κ1​(v)=κ2​(f⁡(v))\kappa_{1}(v)=\kappa_{2}(f(v)). We say F1F_{1} is a subcube of F2F_{2} if there exists an injection g:V⁡(F1)→V⁡(F2)g:V(F_{1})\to V(F_{2}) such that for all v1​v2∈E⁡(F1)v_{1}v_{2}\in E(F_{1}), g⁡(v1)​g​(v2)∈E⁡(F2)g(v_{1})g(v_{2})\in E(F_{2}) and for all v∈V⁡(F1)v\in V(F_{1}) if κ1​(v)=blue\kappa_{1}(v)=\text{blue} then κ2​(g​(v))=blue\kappa_{2}(g(v))=\text{blue}.

The vertex density of F=(n,κ)vF=(n,\kappa)_{v} is

dv(F)=|{v∈V⁡(F):κ⁡(v)=blue}||V⁡(F)|.d_{v}(F)=\frac{|\{v\in V(F):\kappa(v)=\text{blue}\}|}{|V(F)|}.

Note that this is analogous to the hypercube vertex density defined in Section 1. Given a family of vertex-coloured hypercubes ℱ\mathcal{F}, we say HH, a vertex-coloured hypercube, is ℱ\mathcal{F}-free if HH does not contain a subcube isomorphic to any member of ℱ\mathcal{F}. The coloured vertex Turán density of ℱ\mathcal{F} is defined to be the following limit (a simple averaging argument shows that it always exists)

πc​v​(ℱ)=limn→∞maxκ⁡{dv​(H):H=(n,κ)v​ and is ℱ-free}.\pi_{cv}(\mathcal{F})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\max_{\kappa}\{d_{v}(H):H=(n,\kappa)_{v}\textrm{ and is $\mathcal{F}$-free}\}.

Given these definitions it is easy to see that πv​(𝒬3)=πc​v​(B3)\pi_{v}(\mathcal{Q}_{3})=\pi_{cv}(B_{3}), where B3B_{3} is a 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3} with all its vertices coloured blue, see Figure 2. It is also not hard to show that forbidding R2R_{2} in 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} is equivalent to asking that a vertex-coloured hypercube is B3−B_{3}^{-}-free, where B3−B_{3}^{-} is a 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3} with vertex 77 coloured red and the remaining vertices coloured blue, see Figure 2. Hence πv​(R2)=πc​v​(B3−)\pi_{v}(R_{2})=\pi_{cv}(B_{3}^{-}). The final vertex Turán density we will consider is πv​(C6)\pi_{v}(C_{6}) which requires a bit more work to convert into a vertex-coloured hypercube problem. However, it is not too difficult to show that all 66-cycles in 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} lie within a 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3} subgraph and it is easy to check that there are only two distinct 66-cycles in a 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3} up to isomorphism. These two 66-cycles can be represented by two vertex-coloured hypercubes of dimension three which we will call B4B_{4} and B5B_{5} (the names were chosen to be consistent with [1]). Specifically vertices 55 and 77 are coloured red in B4B_{4} and vertices 00 and 77 are red in B5B_{5} (the remaining vertices are blue) see Figure 2. Therefore πv​(C6)=πc​v​(B4,B5)\pi_{v}(C_{6})=\pi_{cv}(B_{4},B_{5}). By extending Razborov’s method to vertex-coloured hypercubes we will be able to prove the following result.

Theorem 2.1.

The following all hold:

  1. (i)

    πv​(R2)=πc​v​(B3−)=2/3\pi_{v}(R_{2})=\pi_{cv}(B_{3}^{-})=2/3,

  2. (ii)

    3/4≤πv​(𝒬3)=πc​v​(B3)≤0.769003/4\leq\pi_{v}(\mathcal{Q}_{3})=\pi_{cv}(B_{3})\leq 0.76900,

  3. (iii)

    1/2≤πv​(C6)=πc​v​(B4,B5)≤0.531111/2\leq\pi_{v}(C_{6})=\pi_{cv}(B_{4},B_{5})\leq 0.53111.

The proofs of the lower bounds in Theorem 2.1 are given by simple constructions. The lower bound of 2/32/3 for πv​(R2)\pi_{v}(R_{2}) is proved by considering the induced subgraph of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} formed by removing every third layer of vertices. Similarly πv​(𝒬3)≥3/4\pi_{v}(\mathcal{Q}_{3})\geq 3/4 and πv​(C6)≥1/2\pi_{v}(C_{6})\geq 1/2 can be proved by looking at 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} with every fourth layer removed and every second layer removed respectively.

The upper bounds in Theorem 2.1 were calculated using Razborov’s semidefinite flag algebra method the details of which are given in the following section (Section 2.1). Specific data for the problems given in Theorem 2.1 can be found in the data files B3-.txt, B3.txt, and B4B5.txt, see [3]. The calculations required to turn the data into upper bounds are too long to do by hand and so we provide the program HypercubeVertexDensityChecker to verify our claims, see [3] (note that the program does not use floating point arithmetic so no rounding errors can occur).

It is worth mentioning that there are many non-isomorphic extremal constructions that are B3−B_{3}^{-}-free and have an asymptotic vertex density of 2/32/3. As far as we are aware this is the first known case where Razborov’s method has given an exact upper bound when there are multiple extremal constructions.

For completeness we will describe the known B3−B_{3}^{-}-free extremal constructions (though there may be more we are unaware of). To create such a construction on 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} first take any partition of the vertices which divides 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} into two disjoint 𝒬n−1\mathcal{Q}_{n-1} subcubes which we will call S1S_{1} and S2S_{2}. Next for each SiS_{i} choose a canonical labelling of its vertices, and an integer zi∈{0,1,2}z_{i}\in\{0,1,2\}. The labelling we chose for each SiS_{i} defines a layering of its vertices, which we will use to colour them. In particular the vertices in layer mm of SiS_{i} are coloured red if m≡zim\equiv z_{i} mod 33 and blue otherwise. It is easy to check that the resulting coloured 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} is B3−B_{3}^{-}-free and asymptotically has 2/32/3 of its vertices coloured blue.

2.1 Razborov’s method on vertex-coloured hypercubes

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a family of coloured hypercubes whose coloured vertex Turán density we wish to compute (or at least approximate). Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be the family of all ℱ\mathcal{F}-free vertex-coloured hypercubes of dimension ll, up to isomorphism. If ll is sufficiently small we can explicitly determine ℋ\mathcal{H} (by computer search if necessary). For H∈ℋH\in\mathcal{H} and a large ℱ\mathcal{F}-free coloured hypercube GG, we define p⁡(H,G)p(H;G) to be the probability that a random hypercube of dimension ll from GG induces a coloured subcube isomorphic to HH.

Trivially, the vertex density of GG is equal to the probability that a random 𝒬0\mathcal{Q}_{0} (a single vertex) from GG is coloured blue. Thus, averaging over hypercubes of dimension ll in GG, we can express the vertex density of GG as

dv​(G)=∑H∈ℋdv​(H)​p​(H,G),\displaystyle d_{v}(G)=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}d_{v}(H)p(H;G), (1)

and hence πc​v​(ℱ)≤maxH∈ℋ⁡dv​(H)\pi_{cv}(\mathcal{F})\leq\max_{H\in\mathcal{H}}d_{v}(H). This “averaging” bound can be improved upon by considering how small pairs of ℱ\mathcal{F}-free hypercubes can intersect and how many times these intersections appear in the HH hypercubes. To utilize this information we will use Razborov’s method and extend his notion of flags and types to hypercubes.

For vertex-coloured hypercubes we define flags and types as follows. A flag, F=(GF,θ)F=(G_{F},\theta), is a vertex-coloured hypercube GFG_{F} together with an injective map θ:{0,1,…,2s−1}→V⁡(GF)\theta:\{0,1,\ldots,2^{s}-1\}\to V(G_{F}) such that θ⁡(i)​θ​(j)∈E⁡(GF)\theta(i)\theta(j)\in E(G_{F}) if and only if ii and jj differ by precisely one digit in their binary representations (i.e. θ\theta induces a canonically labelled hypercube). If θ\theta is bijective (and so |V⁡(GF)|=2s|V(G_{F})|=2^{s}) we call the flag a type. For ease of notation given a flag F=(GF,θ)F=(G_{F},\theta) we define its dimension d​i​m​(F)dim(F) to be the dimension of the hypercube underlying GFG_{F}. Given a type σ\sigma we call a flag F=(GF,θ)F=(G_{F},\theta) a σ\sigma-flag if the induced labelled and coloured subcube of GFG_{F} given by θ\theta is σ\sigma.

Fix a type σ\sigma and an integer m≤(l+d​i​m​(σ))/2m\leq(l+dim(\sigma))/2. (The bound on mm ensures that an ll-dimensional hypercube can contain two mm-dimensional subcubes overlapping in a dimension d​i​m​(σ)dim(\sigma) hypercube.) Let ℱmσ\mathcal{F}^{\sigma}_{m} be the set of all ℱ\mathcal{F}-free σ\sigma-flags of dimension mm, up to isomorphism. Let Θ\Theta be the set of all injective functions from {0,1,…,2d​i​m​(σ)−1}\{0,1,\ldots,2^{dim(\sigma)}-1\} to V⁡(G)V(G), that result in a canonically labelled hypercube. Given F∈ℱmσF\in\mathcal{F}^{\sigma}_{m} and θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta we define p⁡(F,θ,G)p(F,\theta;G) to be the probability that an mm-dimensional coloured hypercube RR chosen uniformly at random from GG subject to im​(θ)⊆V​(R)\text{im}(\theta)\subseteq V(R), induces a σ\sigma-flag (R,θ)(R,\theta) that is isomorphic to FF.

If Fa,Fb∈ℱmσF_{a},F_{b}\in\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\sigma} and θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta then p⁡(Fa,θ,G)​p​(Fb,θ,G)p(F_{a},\theta;G)p(F_{b},\theta;G) is the probability that two mm-dimensional coloured hypercubes Ra,RbR_{a},R_{b} chosen independently at random from GG subject to im​(θ)⊆V⁡(Ra)∩V⁡(Rb)\text{im}(\theta)\subseteq V(R_{a})\cap V(R_{b}), induce σ\sigma-flags (Ra,θ)(R_{a},\theta), (Rb,θ)(R_{b},\theta) that are isomorphic to Fa,FbF_{a},F_{b} respectively. We define the related probability, p⁡(Fa,Fb,θ,G)p(F_{a},F_{b},\theta;G), to be the probability that two mm-dimensional coloured hypercubes Ra,RbR_{a},R_{b} chosen independently at random from GG subject to im​(θ)=V⁡(Ra)∩V⁡(Rb)\text{im}(\theta)=V(R_{a})\cap V(R_{b}), induce σ\sigma-flags (Ra,θ)(R_{a},\theta), (Rb,θ)(R_{b},\theta) that are isomorphic to Fa,FbF_{a},F_{b} respectively. It is easy to show that p⁡(Fa,θ,G)​p​(Fb,θ,G)=p⁡(Fa,Fb,θ,G)+o⁡(1)p(F_{a},\theta;G)p(F_{b},\theta;G)=p(F_{a},F_{b},\theta;G)+o(1) where the o⁡(1)o(1) term vanishes as |V⁡(G)||V(G)| tends to infinity.

Consequently taking the expectation over a uniformly random choice of θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta gives

𝐄θ∈Θ​[p⁡(Fa,θ,G)​p​(Fb,θ,G)]=𝐄θ∈Θ​[p⁡(Fa,Fb,θ,G)]+o⁡(1).\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}\left[p(F_{a},\theta;G)p(F_{b},\theta;G)\right]=\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}\left[p(F_{a},F_{b},\theta;G)\right]+o(1). (2)

Furthermore the expectation on the right hand side of (2) can be rewritten in terms of p⁡(H,G)p(H;G) by averaging over ll-dimensional hypercubes of GG, hence

𝐄θ∈Θ​[p⁡(Fa,θ,G)​p​(Fb,θ,G)]=∑H∈ℋ𝐄θ∈ΘH​[p⁡(Fa,Fb,θ,H)]​p​(H,G)+o⁡(1),\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}\left[p(F_{a},\theta;G)p(F_{b},\theta;G)\right]=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta_{H}}\left[p(F_{a},F_{b},\theta;H)\right]p(H;G)+o(1), (3)

where ΘH\Theta_{H} is the set of all injective maps θ:{0,1,…,2d​i​m​(σ)−1}→V⁡(H)\theta:\{0,1,\ldots,2^{dim(\sigma)}-1\}\to V(H) which induce a canonically labelled hypercube. Note that the right hand side of (3) is a linear combination of p⁡(H,G)p(H;G) terms whose coefficients can be explicitly calculated, this will prove useful when used with (1) which is of a similar form.

Given ℱmσ\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\sigma} and a positive semidefinite matrix Q=(qa​b)Q=(q_{ab}) of dimension |ℱmσ||\mathcal{F}^{\sigma}_{m}|, let 𝐩θ=(p(F,θ;G):F∈ℱmσ)\mathbf{p}_{\theta}=(p(F,\theta;G):F\in\mathcal{F}^{\sigma}_{m}) for θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta. Using (3) and the linearity of expectation we have

0≤𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩θT​Q​𝐩θ]\displaystyle 0\leq\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{\theta}^{T}Q\mathbf{p}_{\theta}] =∑H∈ℋcH​p​(H,G)+o⁡(1)\displaystyle=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}c_{H}p(H;G)+o(1) (4)

where

cH=∑Fa,Fb∈ℱmσqa​b​𝐄θ∈ΘH​[p⁡(Fa,Fb,θ,H)].c_{H}=\sum_{F_{a},F_{b}\in\mathcal{F}^{\sigma}_{m}}q_{ab}\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta_{H}}[p(F_{a},F_{b},\theta;H)].

Note that cHc_{H} is independent of GG and can be explicitly calculated. Combining (4) with (1) allows us to write the following

dv​(G)≤dv​(G)+𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩θT​Q​𝐩θ]=∑H∈ℋ(dv​(H)+cH)​p​(H,G)+o⁡(1).\displaystyle d_{v}(G)\leq d_{v}(G)+\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{\theta}^{T}Q\mathbf{p}_{\theta}]=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}(d_{v}(H)+c_{H})p(H;G)+o(1).

Hence

πc​v​(ℱ)≤maxH∈ℋ⁡(dv​(H)+cH).\pi_{cv}(\mathcal{F})\leq\max_{H\in\mathcal{H}}(d_{v}(H)+c_{H}).

Note that some of the cHc_{H} may be negative and so for a careful choice of QQ this may result in a better bound for the Turán density than the simple “averaging” bound derived from (1). Our task has therefore been reduced to finding an optimal choice of QQ which will lower the bound as much as possible. This is a convex optimization problem in particular a semidefinite programming problem. As such we can use freely available software such as CSDP [8] to find QQ and hence a bound on πc​v​(ℱ)\pi_{cv}(\mathcal{F}).

Our argument can also be extended to consider multiple types σi\sigma_{i}, dimensions mim_{i}, and positive semidefinite matrices QiQ_{i} (of dimension |ℱmiσi||\mathcal{F}_{m_{i}}^{\sigma_{i}}|), to create several terms of the form 𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩i,θT​Qi​𝐩i,θ]\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{i,\theta}^{T}Q_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i,\theta}], where 𝐩i,θ=(p(F,θ;G):F∈ℱmiσi)\mathbf{p}_{i,\theta}=(p(F,\theta;G):F\in\mathcal{F}^{\sigma_{i}}_{m_{i}}). By considering dv​(G)+∑i𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩i,θT​Qi​𝐩i,θ]d_{v}(G)+\sum_{i}\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{i,\theta}^{T}Q_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i,\theta}] we can get a more complicated bound to optimize. However, it is still expressible as a semidefinite program and the extra information often results in a better bound.

It is worth noting that in order to get a tight bound for πc​v​(B3−)\pi_{cv}(B_{3}^{-}) we used the methods described in [1] (Section 2.4.2) to remove the rounding errors. Although the method described in [1] is for hypergraphs, due to its length and the ease in to which it can be converted into the hypercube setting we did not feel it was worth reproducing here.

3 Edge Turán density

In this section we will describe a relatively straightforward extension of Razborov’s method to the edge Turán density problem for hypercubes. Later we will give a more complicated extension using partially defined hypercubes which results in improved bounds.

When we looked at the vertex Turán density problem we found that rather than working directly with subgraphs of hypercubes it was simpler to use vertex-coloured hypercubes instead. Similarly when calculating the edge Turán density we will use red-blue edge-coloured hypercubes to represent subgraphs of hypercubes. The subgraph an edge-coloured hypercube represents can be constructed by removing those edges that are coloured red and keeping those edges that are blue.

We will use the notation (n,κ)e(n,\kappa)_{e} to represent an edge-coloured 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n}, where κ:E(𝒬n)→{red, blue}\kappa:E(\mathcal{Q}_{n})\to\{\text{red, blue}\}. We define V⁡(F)V(F) and E⁡(F)E(F) for an edge-coloured hypercube F=(n,κ)eF=(n,\kappa)_{e} to be V⁡(𝒬n)V(\mathcal{Q}_{n}) and E⁡(𝒬n)E(\mathcal{Q}_{n}) respectively. Consider two edge-coloured hypercubes F1=(n1,κ1)e,F_{1}=(n_{1},\kappa_{1})_{e}, and F2=(n2,κ2)eF_{2}=(n_{2},\kappa_{2})_{e}. We say F1F_{1} is isomorphic to F2F_{2} if there exists a bijection f:V⁡(F1)→V⁡(F2)f:V(F_{1})\to V(F_{2}) such that for all v1​v2∈E⁡(F1)v_{1}v_{2}\in E(F_{1}), f⁡(v1)​f​(v2)∈E⁡(F2)f(v_{1})f(v_{2})\in E(F_{2}) and κ1​(v1​v2)=κ2​(f⁡(v1)​f​(v2))\kappa_{1}(v_{1}v_{2})=\kappa_{2}(f(v_{1})f(v_{2})). We say F1F_{1} is a subcube of F2F_{2} if there exists an injection g:V⁡(F1)→V⁡(F2)g:V(F_{1})\to V(F_{2}) such that for all v1​v2∈E⁡(F1)v_{1}v_{2}\in E(F_{1}), g⁡(v1)​g​(v2)∈E⁡(F2)g(v_{1})g(v_{2})\in E(F_{2}) and if κ1​(v1​v2)=blue\kappa_{1}(v_{1}v_{2})=\text{blue} then κ2​(g⁡(v1)​g​(v2))=blue\kappa_{2}(g(v_{1})g(v_{2}))=\text{blue}.

The edge density of F=(n,κ)eF=(n,\kappa)_{e} is

de(F)=|{v1​v2∈E⁡(F):κ⁡(v1​v2)=blue}||E⁡(F)|.d_{e}(F)=\frac{|\{v_{1}v_{2}\in E(F):\kappa(v_{1}v_{2})=\text{blue}\}|}{|E(F)|}.

Note that this is analogous to the hypercube edge density defined in Section 1. Given a family of coloured hypercubes ℱ\mathcal{F}, we say HH, a coloured hypercube, is ℱ\mathcal{F}-free if HH does not contain a subcube isomorphic to any member of ℱ\mathcal{F}. The coloured edge Turán density of ℱ\mathcal{F} is defined to be the following limit (a simple averaging argument shows that it always exists)

πc​e​(ℱ)=limn→∞maxκ⁡{de​(H):H=(n,κ)e​ and is ℱ-free}.\pi_{ce}(\mathcal{F})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\max_{\kappa}\{d_{e}(H):H=(n,\kappa)_{e}\textrm{ and is $\mathcal{F}$-free}\}.

Given these definitions it is easy to see that πe​(𝒬2)=πc​e​(B)\pi_{e}(\mathcal{Q}_{2})=\pi_{ce}(B) where BB is a 𝒬2\mathcal{Q}_{2} with all four of its edges coloured blue, see Figure 3. We are also interested in πe​(C6)\pi_{e}(C_{6}). It is not to difficult to show that all 66-cycles in 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} lie within a 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3} subgraph. There are two distinct 66-cycles in a 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3} up to isomorphism, their edge sets are E1={01,13,32,26,64,40}E_{1}=\{01,13,32,26,64,40\}, and E2={51,13,32,26,64,45}E_{2}=\{51,13,32,26,64,45\}. Let B1B_{1} be a 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3} with those edges in E1E_{1} coloured blue and the remaining edges coloured red, see Figure 3. Similarly let B2B_{2} be a 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3} with those edges in E2E_{2} coloured blue and the remaining edges coloured red, see Figure 3. Hence forbidding a blue edged 66-cycle in an edge-coloured hypercube is equivalent to requiring that it is B1B_{1} and B2B_{2}-free. Therefore πe​(C6)=πc​e​(B1,B2)\pi_{e}(C_{6})=\pi_{ce}(B_{1},B_{2}). By extending Razborov’s semidefinite flag algebra method to edge-coloured hypercubes, we will be able to prove the following bounds on πc​e​(B)\pi_{ce}(B) and πc​e​(B1,B2)\pi_{ce}(B_{1},B_{2}).

Theorem 3.1.

πe​(𝒬2)=πc​e​(B)≤0.60680\pi_{e}(\mathcal{Q}_{2})=\pi_{ce}(B)\leq 0.60680 and πe​(C6)=πc​e​(B1,B2)≤0.37550\pi_{e}(C_{6})=\pi_{ce}(B_{1},B_{2})\leq 0.37550.

We omit the details of extending Razborov’s technique to edge-coloured hypercubes; it is virtually identical to the extension described in Section 2.1, with the term “edge-coloured” replacing the term “vertex-coloured”.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

All the necessary data (types, flags, matrices, etc.) needed to prove πc​e​(B)≤0.60680\pi_{ce}(B)\leq 0.60680 can be found in the file B.txt [2]. The calculation that converts this data into an upper bound is too long to do by hand and so we provide the program HypercubeEdgeDensityChecker (see [2]) to verify our claim (the program does not use floating point arithmetic so no rounding errors can occur). Similarly the data needed to prove πc​e​(B1,B2)≤0.37550\pi_{ce}(B_{1},B_{2})\leq 0.37550 can be found in the file B1B2.txt [2]. ∎

4 Partially defined hypercubes

In this section we improve the bounds given in Theorem 3.1 by applying a slightly modified version of Razborov’s method to partially defined hypercubes. We define a partially defined hypercube simply to be an edge-coloured hypercube where instead of colouring the edges with just two colours, red and blue, we use three colours, red, blue, and grey. Note that throughout this section we will use the less cumbersome term red-blue hypercube to refer to red-blue edge-coloured hypercubes (as defined in Section 3).

The interpretation we gave to a red-blue hypercube in Section 3 was that it represented a subgraph whilst retaining the underlying structure of the hypercube. The subgraph could be reconstructed by removing those edges which are red, and keeping those which are blue. We have a similar interpretation for partially defined hypercubes, as before those edges that are red or blue represent edges to remove or keep respectively, but grey edges represent edges which are undefined (i.e. the colouring does not specify whether to remove the edge or not). Hence a partially defined hypercube does not represent a single subgraph but a set of subgraphs.

The use of grey edges causes us to lose some information that could be useful in bounding the Turán density, but it also reduces the size of the computations which we can use to our advantage. To illustrate this point further we first note that in order to calculate the upper bound for πc​e​(B)\pi_{ce}(B) using Razborov’s method we need to explicitly determine ℋ\mathcal{H} the family of all ll-dimensional BB-free red-blue hypercubes for some choice of ll. The size of ℋ\mathcal{H} gives us a rough indication of how hard the computation will be. To get the bound given in Theorem 3.1 we looked at 33-dimensional red-blue hypercubes (i.e. l=3l=3) which results in |ℋ|=99|\mathcal{H}|=99, and consequently the computation is very quick on most computers. We can achieve a better bound by looking at 44-dimensional red-blue hypercubes but this unfortunately results in |ℋ|=3212821|\mathcal{H}|=3212821 which is currently computationally unfeasible on an average computer. However, by looking at 44-dimensional partially defined hypercubes we can reduce |ℋ||\mathcal{H}| to the more feasible value of 9017990179 and still make use of some of the information held in red-blue hypercubes of dimension 44. In fact we have some choice over how many grey edges our partially defined hypercubes will contain which translates into some control over how large we wish to make |ℋ||\mathcal{H}| and how difficult a computation we want to attempt.

In this section we are primarily going to consider a very specific type of partially defined hypercube, namely ones where if i​jij is an edge then it is grey if and only if |i−j|=1|i-j|=1, see Figure 4 for an example. We will refer to such a partially defined hypercube simply as a partial hypercube.

By applying a slightly modified version of Razborov’s method to partial hypercubes we can improve the bounds given in Theorem 3.1.

Theorem 4.1.

πe​(𝒬2)=πc​e​(B)≤0.60318\pi_{e}(\mathcal{Q}_{2})=\pi_{ce}(B)\leq 0.60318 and πe​(C6)=πc​e​(B1,B2)≤0.36577\pi_{e}(C_{6})=\pi_{ce}(B_{1},B_{2})\leq 0.36577.

The relevant data files PartialB.txt, PartialB1B2.txt, and the program PartialHypercubeEdgeDensityChecker used for verification purposes can be found in the source files section on the arXiv see [4].

The rest of this section will be devoted to explaining the technical details of extending flag algebras to partial hypercubes. We will extend Razborov’s method to partial hypercubes in the simplest and most obvious way in Section 4.1. Unfortunately this extension does not produce better bounds than those given in Theorem 3.1. We will remedy this in Section 4.2 by incorporating some extra constraints into the method.

4.1 Razborov’s method on partial hypercubes

We will begin with some basic definitions. Note that the definitions and explanations will involve red-blue hypercubes as defined in Section 3 so care must be taken to avoid confusion.

We will use the notation (n,κ)p(n,\kappa)_{p} to formally represent an nn-dimensional partial hypercube, where κ:E⁡(𝒬n)→{red, blue, grey}\kappa:E(\mathcal{Q}_{n})\to\{\text{red, blue, grey}\}, and κ⁡(v1​v2)=grey\kappa(v_{1}v_{2})=\text{grey} if and only if |v1−v2|=1|v_{1}-v_{2}|=1. We define V⁡(F)V(F) and E⁡(F)E(F) for a partial hypercube F=(n,κ)pF=(n,\kappa)_{p} to be V⁡(𝒬n)V(\mathcal{Q}_{n}) and E⁡(𝒬n)E(\mathcal{Q}_{n}) respectively. Consider two partial hypercubes F1=(n1,κ1)p,F_{1}=(n_{1},\kappa_{1})_{p}, and F2=(n2,κ2)pF_{2}=(n_{2},\kappa_{2})_{p}. We say F1F_{1} is isomorphic to F2F_{2} if there exists a bijection f:V⁡(F1)→V⁡(F2)f:V(F_{1})\to V(F_{2}) such that for all v1​v2∈E⁡(F1)v_{1}v_{2}\in E(F_{1}), f⁡(v1)​f​(v2)∈E⁡(F2)f(v_{1})f(v_{2})\in E(F_{2}) and κ1​(v1​v2)=κ2​(f⁡(v1)​f​(v2))\kappa_{1}(v_{1}v_{2})=\kappa_{2}(f(v_{1})f(v_{2})). The edge density of F=(n,κ)pF=(n,\kappa)_{p} is

dp(F)=|{v1​v2∈E⁡(F):κ⁡(v1​v2)=blue}||{v1​v2∈E⁡(F):κ⁡(v1​v2)≠grey}|.d_{p}(F)=\frac{|\{v_{1}v_{2}\in E(F):\kappa(v_{1}v_{2})=\text{blue}\}|}{|\{v_{1}v_{2}\in E(F):\kappa(v_{1}v_{2})\neq\text{grey}\}|}.

To ease notation later we define 𝒫\mathcal{P} to be a function which converts red-blue hypercubes to partial hypercubes by colouring some edges grey. In particular 𝒫⁡((n,κ)e)=(n,κ′)p\mathcal{P}((n,\kappa)_{e})=(n,\kappa^{\prime})_{p} where κ′​(v1​v2)=grey\kappa^{\prime}(v_{1}v_{2})=\text{grey} if |v1−v2|=1|v_{1}-v_{2}|=1 and κ′​(v1​v2)=κ⁡(v1​v2)\kappa^{\prime}(v_{1}v_{2})=\kappa(v_{1}v_{2}) otherwise.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the family of red-blue hypercubes, for which we are trying to compute an upper bound of πc​e​(ℱ)\pi_{ce}(\mathcal{F}).

In the red-blue hypercube case our application of Razborov’s method involved computing ℋ\mathcal{H} the family of all ℱ\mathcal{F}-free red-blue hypercubes of dimension ll up to isomorphism (for some choice of ll). In the partial hypercube version of Razborov’s method, ℋ\mathcal{H} will be a family of partial hypercubes, and we will require that it retain the key property that it represents all the possible ll-dimensional subcubes that could appear in a large ℱ\mathcal{F}-free red-blue hypercube. With this in mind we make the following definitions. We say a partial hypercube (n,κ)p(n,\kappa)_{p} is ℱ\mathcal{F}-free if (n,κ′)e(n,\kappa^{\prime})_{e} is ℱ\mathcal{F}-free where κ′​(v1​v2)=red\kappa^{\prime}(v_{1}v_{2})=\text{red} if κ⁡(v1​v2)=grey\kappa(v_{1}v_{2})=\text{grey} and κ′​(v1​v2)=κ⁡(v1​v2)\kappa^{\prime}(v_{1}v_{2})=\kappa(v_{1}v_{2}) otherwise. Using this we define ℋ\mathcal{H} to be the family of ℱ\mathcal{F}-free partial hypercubes of dimension ll, up to isomorphism.

For H∈ℋH\in\mathcal{H} and a large ℱ\mathcal{F}-free red-blue hypercube GG, we define p⁡(H,G)p(H;G) to be the probability that a random hypercube of dimension ll from GG, together with a random canonical labelling of its vertices, induces a coloured red-blue subcube H′H^{\prime} such that 𝒫⁡(H′)\mathcal{P}(H^{\prime}) is isomorphic to HH. Note that ∑H∈ℋp⁡(H,G)=1\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}p(H;G)=1. Trivially, the edge density of GG is equal to the probability that a random edge from GG is coloured blue. Thus, averaging over partial hypercubes of dimension ll in GG, we can express the edge density of GG as

de​(G)=∑H∈ℋdp​(H)​p​(H,G),\displaystyle d_{e}(G)=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}d_{p}(H)p(H;G), (5)

(provided l≥2l\geq 2) and hence πc​e​(ℱ)≤maxH∈ℋ⁡dp​(H)\pi_{ce}(\mathcal{F})\leq\max_{H\in\mathcal{H}}d_{p}(H). This bound can be improved upon by considering how small pairs of ℱ\mathcal{F}-free partial hypercubes can intersect, we use Razborov’s notion of flags and types to describe and utilize this information.

For partial hypercubes we define flags and types as follows. A flag, F=(GF,θ)F=(G_{F},\theta), is a partial hypercube GF=(n,κ)pG_{F}=(n,\kappa)_{p} for some n≥1n\geq 1 and κ\kappa, together with an injective map θ:{0,1,…,2s−1}→V⁡(GF)\theta:\{0,1,\ldots,2^{s}-1\}\to V(G_{F}) for some s≥1s\geq 1, such that θ⁡(i)​θ​(j)∈E⁡(GF)\theta(i)\theta(j)\in E(G_{F}) if and only if ii and jj differ by precisely one digit in their binary representations and κ⁡(θ⁡(i)​θ​(j))=grey\kappa(\theta(i)\theta(j))=\text{grey} when |i−j|=1|i-j|=1 (i.e. θ\theta induces a canonically labelled partial hypercube). If θ\theta is bijective (and so |V⁡(GF)|=2s|V(G_{F})|=2^{s}) we call the flag a type. For ease of notation given a flag F=(GF,θ)F=(G_{F},\theta) we define its dimension d​i​m​(F)dim(F) to be the dimension of the hypercube underlying GFG_{F}. Given a type σ\sigma we call a flag F=(GF,θ)F=(G_{F},\theta) a σ\sigma-flag if the induced labelled partial subcube of GFG_{F} given by θ\theta is σ\sigma.

We define ℱmσ\mathcal{F}^{\sigma}_{m} be the set of all ℱ\mathcal{F}-free σ\sigma-flags of dimension mm, up to isomorphism (where m≤(l+d​i​m​(σ))/2m\leq(l+dim(\sigma))/2). Let Θ\Theta be the set of all injective functions from {0,1,…,2d​i​m​(σ)−1}\{0,1,\ldots,2^{dim(\sigma)}-1\} to V⁡(G)V(G), that result in a canonically labelled hypercube. Given F∈ℱmσF\in\mathcal{F}^{\sigma}_{m} and θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta we define p⁡(F,θ,G)p(F,\theta;G) to be the probability that an mm-dimensional hypercube RR chosen uniformly at random from GG subject to im​(θ)⊆V​(R)\text{im}(\theta)\subseteq V(R) induces a σ\sigma-flag with labelled vertices given by θ\theta that is isomorphic to FF.

Given 𝐩θ=(p(F,θ;G):F∈ℱmσ)\mathbf{p}_{\theta}=(p(F,\theta;G):F\in\mathcal{F}^{\sigma}_{m}), and QQ a positive semidefinite matrix, we can show 𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩θT​Q​𝐩θ]\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{\theta}^{T}Q\mathbf{p}_{\theta}] is non-negative and can be written explicitly in terms of p⁡(H,G)p(H;G) for H∈ℋH\in\mathcal{H}. We omit the details as the argument is virtually identical to that given in Section 2.1. As before we can consider multiple types σi\sigma_{i}, and positive semidefinite matrices QiQ_{i} to create multiple terms of the form 𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩i,θT​Qi​𝐩i,θ]\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{i,\theta}^{T}Q_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i,\theta}] which will result in better bounds on πc​e​(ℱ)\pi_{ce}(\mathcal{F}). Let

∑i𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩i,θT​Qi​𝐩i,θ]=∑H∈ℋcH​p​(H,G)+o⁡(1),\displaystyle\sum_{i}{\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{i,\theta}^{T}Q_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i,\theta}]}=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}c_{H}p(H;G)+o(1), (6)

where cHc_{H} can be explicitly calculated from HH, and the o⁡(1)o(1) term vanishes as |V⁡(G)||V(G)| tends to infinity. Using (6) together with the fact that the QiQ_{i} are positive semidefinite, and applying it to (5) gives us

de​(G)≤de​(G)+∑i𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩i,θT​Qi​𝐩i,θ]=∑H∈ℋ(dp​(H)+cH)​p​(H,G)+o⁡(1).\displaystyle d_{e}(G)\leq d_{e}(G)+\sum_{i}{\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{i,\theta}^{T}Q_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i,\theta}]}=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}(d_{p}(H)+c_{H})p(H;G)+o(1). (7)

Therefore

πc​e​(ℱ)≤maxH∈ℋ⁡(dp​(H)+cH).\pi_{ce}(\mathcal{F})\leq\max_{H\in\mathcal{H}}(d_{p}(H)+c_{H}).

The matrices QiQ_{i} and hence the optimal bound on πc​e​(ℱ)\pi_{ce}(\mathcal{F}) can be determined by solving a semidefinite program.

4.2 Additional constraints

Unfortunately the method as it stands does not perform well. Considering ll-dimensional ℱ\mathcal{F}-free partial hypercubes produces precisely the same bound as considering (l−1)(l-1)-dimensional red-blue hypercubes and the latter results in a significantly easier computation. The reason for this lack of improvement is that the semidefinite program we create does not encode that we are looking at ll-dimensional partial hypercubes. We get the same semidefinite program by instead looking at any two (l−1)(l-1)-dimensional red-blue subcubes of GG artificially made into a partial hypercube by adding grey edges between them. To be clear, in this case we do not require that the two (l−1)(l-1)-dimensional red-blue hypercubes come from the same ll-dimensional hypercube (whereas in the partial hypercube case we do). Consequently we gain no extra information that was not already given in (l−1)(l-1)-dimensional red-blue hypercubes, and hence no improvement in the bound.

We remedy this situation by introducing some linear constraints of the form ∑H∈ℋaH​p​(H,G)=0\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}a_{H}p(H;G)=0 which hold for all ℱ\mathcal{F}-free GG, and the coefficients aHa_{H} can be explicitly calculated from the partial hypercubes H∈ℋH\in\mathcal{H}. Given a set of such constraints ∑H∈ℋaj,H​p​(H,G)=0\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}a_{j,H}p(H;G)=0, indexed by jj, and an associated set of real values μj\mu_{j} we have

0=∑jμj​∑H∈ℋaj,H​p​(H,G)=∑H∈ℋαH​p​(H,G)\displaystyle 0=\sum_{j}\mu_{j}\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}a_{j,H}p(H;G)=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}\alpha_{H}p(H;G)

where αH=∑jμj​aj,H\alpha_{H}=\sum_{j}\mu_{j}a_{j,H}. Applying this to (7) gives us

de​(G)≤∑H∈ℋ(dp​(H)+cH+αH)​p​(H,G)+o⁡(1),d_{e}(G)\leq\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}(d_{p}(H)+c_{H}+\alpha_{H})p(H;G)+o(1),

which implies a potentially better bound of

πc​e​(ℱ)≤maxH∈ℋ⁡(dp​(H)+cH+αH).\pi_{ce}(\mathcal{F})\leq\max_{H\in\mathcal{H}}(d_{p}(H)+c_{H}+\alpha_{H}).

Note that we can still pose the question of determining the optimal semidefinite matrices and coefficients μj\mu_{j} as a single semidefinite program.

The linear constraints we will use come from calculating the probabilities of various partially defined hypercubes appearing in GG. Let us define 𝒮\mathcal{S} to be the set of all red-blue-grey edge-coloured 𝒬l\mathcal{Q}_{l} (where ll is the dimension of the H∈ℋH\in\mathcal{H}) with the property that i​j∈E⁡(𝒬l)ij\in E(\mathcal{Q}_{l}) is coloured grey if and only if |i−j|=1|i-j|=1 or 22 (note that such partially defined hypercubes are not partial hypercubes). We will show for each S∈𝒮S\in\mathcal{S} we can form a linear constraint of the required form ∑aH​p​(H,G)=0\sum a_{H}p(H;G)=0, but first we require some definitions.

We say an edge i​j∈E⁡(𝒬l)ij\in E(\mathcal{Q}_{l}) lies across dimension dd if |i−j|=2d|i-j|=2^{d}. Define a 𝒬l\mathcal{Q}_{l}-mapping to be a bijective function ϕ:V⁡(𝒬l)→V⁡(𝒬l)\phi:V(\mathcal{Q}_{l})\to V(\mathcal{Q}_{l}) satisfying i​j∈E⁡(𝒬l)ij\in E(\mathcal{Q}_{l}) if and only if ϕ⁡(i)​ϕ​(j)∈E⁡(𝒬l)\phi(i)\phi(j)\in E(\mathcal{Q}_{l}). Given a,b∈{0,…,l−1}a,b\in\{0,\ldots,l-1\} define ϕa​b\phi_{ab} to be the 𝒬l\mathcal{Q}_{l}-mapping where the binary representation of ϕa​b​(i)\phi_{ab}(i) is the same as that of ii but with bits aa and bb swapped (we take bit 00 to be the least significant bit). Note that the effect of ϕa​b\phi_{ab} is to swap the edges that lie across dimension aa with those that lie across dimension bb. Let Φ\Phi be the set of all 𝒬l\mathcal{Q}_{l}-mappings ϕ\phi that satisfy for all i​j∈E⁡(𝒬l)ij\in E(\mathcal{Q}_{l}) with |i−j|=1|i-j|=1 or 22, |i−j|=|ϕ⁡(i)−ϕ⁡(j)||i-j|=|\phi(i)-\phi(j)|. In other words Φ\Phi consists of all 𝒬l\mathcal{Q}_{l}-mappings which keeps those edges lying across dimension 00 or 11 still lying across dimension 00 or 11 respectively. Given two ll-dimensional partially defined hypercubes F1,F2F_{1},F_{2}, we say F1F_{1} is isomorphic to F2F_{2} under Φ\Phi if there exists ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi such that the colour of every edge i​jij in F1F_{1} matches that of ϕ⁡(i)​ϕ​(j)\phi(i)\phi(j) in F2F_{2}. Recall that in Section 4.1 we defined the function 𝒫\mathcal{P} to convert red-blue hypercubes into partial hypercubes by recolouring the edges that lie across dimension 00 to grey. We similarly define 𝒫′\mathcal{P}^{\prime} to be a function which recolours the edges that lie across dimension 00 or 11 to grey. Finally, given a 𝒬l\mathcal{Q}_{l}-mapping ϕ\phi and a partially defined hypercube FF of dimension ll, we will abuse notation and take ϕ⁡(F)\phi(F) to be a partially defined hypercube of dimension ll with edge ϕ⁡(i)​ϕ​(j)\phi(i)\phi(j) in ϕ⁡(F)\phi(F) having the same colour as i​jij in FF.

Given S∈𝒮S\in\mathcal{S} we will form our linear constraint by considering pΦ​(S,G)p_{\Phi}(S;G) the probability that a random hypercube of dimension ll from GG, together with a random canonical labelling of its vertices, induces a coloured red-blue subcube S′S^{\prime} such that 𝒫′​(S′)\mathcal{P}^{\prime}(S^{\prime}) is isomorphic to SS under Φ\Phi. We can calculate pΦ​(S,G)p_{\Phi}(S;G) explicitly in terms of p⁡(H,G)p(H;G) by taking S′S^{\prime} then applying 𝒫\mathcal{P} to get a partial hypercube H∈ℋH\in\mathcal{H}. With probability p⁡(H,G)p(H;G), 𝒫⁡(S′)\mathcal{P}(S^{\prime}) is isomorphic to HH, so we can write

pΦ​(S,G)=∑H∈ℋpΦ​(S,H)​p​(H,G)p_{\Phi}(S;G)=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}p_{\Phi}(S;H)p(H;G)

where pΦ​(S,H)p_{\Phi}(S;H) is the probability that 𝒫′​(ϕ1​n​(H))\mathcal{P}^{\prime}(\phi_{1n}(H)) is isomorphic to SS under Φ\Phi for some random choice of nn from {1,…,l−1}\{1,\ldots,l-1\} (we interpret ϕ11\phi_{11} as the identity map).

It should be clear that since pΦ​(S,G)p_{\Phi}(S;G) involves looking at a random red-blue hypercube, that pΦ​(S,G)=pΦ​(ϕ01​(S),G)p_{\Phi}(S;G)=p_{\Phi}(\phi_{01}(S);G) and both the left and right hand sides can be written in terms of p⁡(H,G)p(H;G) giving us the linear constraint

∑H∈ℋ(pΦ​(S,H)−pΦ​(ϕ01​(S),H))​p​(H,G)=0\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}\big(p_{\Phi}(S;H)-p_{\Phi}(\phi_{01}(S);H)\big)p(H;G)=0

as desired.

5 Other partially defined objects

In Section 4 we gave a concrete example of using partially defined graphs to improve a bound. In particular the graph was a hypercube and we chose our undefined edges in a very particular way. It is worth noting that there are many other ways we could have chosen the undefined edges, for example we could have said that an edge v1​v2v_{1}v_{2} is grey if and only if both v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} are odd. Alternatively we could have taken ℋ\mathcal{H} to be all red-blue-grey edge-coloured hypercubes with precisely tt grey edges for some fixed choice of tt. This choice of how we choose the undefined edges gives us some control of the size of the computation and the improvement in the bound of the Turán density we can expect. We by no means think that Theorem 4.1 gives the best possible bounds using partial hypercubes, however the description of partial hypercubes we used gave us a reasonable improvement and applying Razborov’s method to it was not too difficult.

Although so far we have only looked at Turán density problems on hypercubes it should be clear that the method of using partially defined objects will work in most of the applications Razborov’s method has been applied. As an example we will briefly describe one way it can be used in the case of 33-uniform hypergraphs, or 33-graphs for short.

5.1 Partially defined 33-graphs

We will pick our undefined edges in the following way, choose two distinct vertices uu, vv from the 33-graph and make every triple containing precisely one of {u,v}\{u,v\} an undefined edge. Such partially defined graphs have the nice property that if we remove uu, and vv we get a fully defined standard 33-graph the only information we have lost is from edges and non-edges of the form u​v​wuvw, which we can recover by colouring vertex ww red and blue say to represent whether u​v​wuvw was a non-edge or an edge respectively. Hence we can represent our partially defined 33-graphs as red-blue vertex-coloured 33-graphs. Note that linear constraints such as those given in Section 4.2 are still needed to encode that the coloured vertices represent edges and non-edges, these can be obtained by again calculating the probabilities of partially defined graphs appearing in two different ways.

We have used such partially defined graphs to improve the bound of π⁡(K43)\pi(K_{4}^{3}), the Turán density of the complete 33-graph on 44 vertices. The best known bound was held by Razborov [18] at 0.561670.56167 by considering 33-graphs of order 66. We can decrease this to 0.56150.5615 by looking at red-blue vertex-coloured 33-graphs of order 66, together with regularity constraints as described by Hladký, Král’, and Norine [13]. We will describe the regularity constraints in more detail in Section 5.1.1. The relevant data required to prove the 0.56150.5615 bound can be found in K4.txt located in the source files section on the arXiv, see [4].

Although the amount we have decreased the bound by is not that impressive, a significantly better bound may be possible, as due to time restrictions we did not make full use of the information contained in the flags. In particular we chose to ignore the colours of the non-labelled vertices. This was achieved by redefining a flag to be a (partially labelled) red-blue-grey vertex-coloured 33-graph, where the non-labelled vertices are coloured grey to represent undefined edges.

It is important to note that there are many alternative types of partially defined 33-graphs we could try instead of red-blue vertex coloured 33-graphs, any one of which may result in a significant improvement to the bound of π⁡(K43)\pi(K_{4}^{3}). Our choice to use red-blue vertex-coloured 33-graphs was motivated only by the fact that it would be simple to explain and implement.

5.1.1 Regularity constraints

Our proof that π⁡(K43)≤0.5615\pi(K_{4}^{3})\leq 0.5615 involves regularity constraints such as those described by Hladký, Král’, and Norine for digraphs [13]. In this section we will describe the constraints and show they can be applied to the problem of bounding π⁡(ℱ)\pi(\mathcal{F}) for any forbidden family of covering 33-graphs ℱ\mathcal{F}. A graph is said to be covering if every pair of vertices belong to an edge.

To get a bound for π⁡(ℱ)\pi(\mathcal{F}) Razborov’s method involves looking at a large ℱ\mathcal{F}-free graph GG to get a bound for the density d⁡(G)d(G). By considering a sequence of edge maximal ℱ\mathcal{F}-free graphs of increasing order, d⁡(G)d(G) can be made to tend to π⁡(ℱ)\pi(\mathcal{F}) thereby giving us a bound on the Turán density. We will instead work with a sequence of ℱ\mathcal{F}-free graphs {Gn}n=1∞\{G_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}, which have the property that |V⁡(Gn)|=n|V(G_{n})|=n, and (1−o⁡(1))​n(1-o(1))n of the vertices of GnG_{n} have a degree density which is at most o⁡(1)o(1) from ρ\rho for some fixed value ρ\rho, where o⁡(1)o(1) tends to 00 as nn tends to infinity. (We define the degree density of a vertex vv to be the number of edges containing vv divided by the number of triples containing vv.) We will begin by showing that for any non-negative ρ≤π⁡(ℱ)\rho\leq\pi(\mathcal{F}) there exists just such a sequence of graphs. Hence when we apply Razborov’s method to GnG_{n} we can not only assume it is ℱ\mathcal{F}-free but that it is also almost regular (in a very precise sense) which is a condition we can use to achieve a better upper bound.

We will create {Gn}n=1∞\{G_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} from {Mn}n=1∞\{M_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} a sequence of extremal ℱ\mathcal{F}-free graphs with |V⁡(Mn)|=n|V(M_{n})|=n and |E⁡(Mn)|=e​x​(n,ℱ)|E(M_{n})|=ex(n,\mathcal{F}). The difference between the maximum and minimum degree density in MnM_{n} can be at most 2/(n−1)2/(n-1) otherwise removing the vertex with the minimum degree density and cloning the vertex with the maximum degree density would result in an nn vertex graph that is ℱ\mathcal{F}-free and has more edges than MnM_{n}. It is trivial to check that the average degree density is d⁡(Mn)d(M_{n}) and hence every vertex in MnM_{n} has a degree density between d⁡(Mn)+2/(n−1)d(M_{n})+2/(n-1) and d⁡(Mn)−2/(n−1)d(M_{n})-2/(n-1). We can take MnM_{n} and randomly remove each of its edges with probability 1−ρ/d⁡(Mn)1-\rho/d(M_{n}) (recall that ρ≤π⁡(ℱ)≤d⁡(Mn)\rho\leq\pi(\mathcal{F})\leq d(M_{n}) so this is a valid probability). An application of Chebyshev’s inequality shows that there must exist a way of removing edges from MnM_{n} such that (1−o⁡(1))​n(1-o(1))n of the vertices will have a degree density that is at most n−12n^{-\frac{1}{2}} from their expected degree density (which is their degree density in MnM_{n} multiplied by ρ/d⁡(Mn)\rho/d(M_{n})). In other words (1−o⁡(1))​n(1-o(1))n of the vertices will have degree density ρ+o⁡(1)\rho+o(1) as required.

Let σ\sigma be the type of order 11 (a single labelled vertex), and Let FF be the σ\sigma-flag of order 33 whose underlying graph is a single edge (just to be clear here we are considering flags and types to be simple uncoloured graphs). Since GnG_{n} is almost regular we know that for most choices of θ\theta we have p⁡(F,θ,Gn)=ρ+o⁡(1)p(F,\theta;G_{n})=\rho+o(1). In fact for any σ\sigma-flag CC, we have p⁡(C,F,θ,Gn)=ρ​p​(C,θ,Gn)+o⁡(1)p(C,F,\theta;G_{n})=\rho p(C,\theta;G_{n})+o(1) for (1−o⁡(1))​n(1-o(1))n choices of θ\theta. Hence

𝐄θ∈Θ​[p⁡(C,F,θ,Gn)−ρ​p​(C,θ,Gn)]=o⁡(1)\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[p(C,F,\theta;G_{n})-\rho p(C,\theta;G_{n})]=o(1)

and the left hand side can be expressed explicitly in terms of p⁡(H,Gn)p(H;G_{n}). Clearly for every σ\sigma-flag CC we can construct such a constraint, which we will refer to as a regularity constraint.

By summing a linear combination of regularity constraints as well as terms of the form 𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩θT​Q​𝐩θ]\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{\theta}^{T}Q\mathbf{p}_{\theta}] we can create an expression which can be written explicitly in terms of p⁡(H,Gn)p(H;G_{n}), and is asymptotically non-negative provided ρ≤π⁡(ℱ)\rho\leq\pi(\mathcal{F}). For a given ρ\rho the problem of finding the optimal linear combination of the regularity constraints and positive semidefinite matrices QQ that minimize the coefficients of p⁡(H,Gn)p(H;G_{n}) can be posed as a semidefinite programming problem. If all the coefficients of p⁡(H,Gn)p(H;G_{n}) can be made strictly negative a contradiction occurs implying ρ\rho must in fact be an upper bound for π⁡(ℱ)\pi(\mathcal{F}).

Note that finding the optimal upper bound of π⁡(ℱ)\pi(\mathcal{F}) is not a semidefinite programming problem but testing whether a specific value is an upper bound is a semidefinite programming problem. It can be proven (though we will not do so here) that if the semidefinite program shows ρ\rho to be an upper bound then it will also show ρ′\rho^{\prime} to be an upper bound for any ρ′≥ρ\rho^{\prime}\geq\rho. This allows us to carry out a binary search to determine the optimal bound to whatever accuracy we wish.

Extending this method to use partially defined graphs is a trivial matter. The coefficients of p⁡(H,Gn)p(H;G_{n}) for the regularity constraints can still be explicitly calculated even when HH is a vertex-coloured 33-graph. In fact calculating the probability of the intersection of CC and FF appearing is equivalent to considering the occurrence of the vertex-coloured flag formed from CC by colouring the labelled vertex blue, and the other vertices grey. This allows us to construct regularity constraints from larger σ\sigma-flags, which in turn means we can add many more regularity constraints into our semidefinite program. Because we are using partially defined graphs we also need to include additional constraints similar to those described in Section 4.2. Since such constraints are of the form ∑H∈ℋaH​p​(H,G)=0\sum_{H\in\mathcal{H}}a_{H}p(H;G)=0 we can incorporate them into the semidefinite program in the same way as the regularity constraints.

6 Open problems and future work

The power of using partially defined graphs comes from being able to reduce the size of ℋ\mathcal{H} to make computations more feasible. Another way we could do this is the following. Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a family of ℱ\mathcal{F}-free graphs we wish to reduce and let ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} be a family of subsets of ℋ\mathcal{H} that partition ℋ\mathcal{H}, i.e. ⋃H′∈ℋ′H′=ℋ\bigcup_{H^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}^{\prime}}H^{\prime}=\mathcal{H} and for all distinct H1′,H2′∈ℋ′H_{1}^{\prime},H_{2}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}^{\prime} we have H1′∩H2′=∅H_{1}^{\prime}\cap H_{2}^{\prime}=\emptyset. Now instead of applying Razborov’s semidefinite flag algebra technique to H∈ℋH\in\mathcal{H} we can apply it to H′∈ℋ′H^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H^{\prime}}. We can define p⁡(H′,G)p(H^{\prime};G) to be ∑H∈H′p⁡(H,G)\sum_{H\in H^{\prime}}p(H;G). There is some difficulty in expressing quantities like the products of flags 𝐄θ∈Θ​[p⁡(Fa,Fb,θ,G)]\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[p(F_{a},F_{b},\theta;G)] in terms of a linear sum of p⁡(H′,G)p(H^{\prime};G). However, we can overcome this by bounding the coefficients above and below, for example

∑H′∈ℋ′cm​i​n,H′​p​(H′,G)≤𝐄θ∈Θ​[p⁡(Fa,Fb,θ,G)]≤∑H′∈ℋ′cm​a​x,H′​p​(H′,G)\displaystyle\sum_{H^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}^{\prime}}c_{min,H^{\prime}}p(H^{\prime};G)\leq\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[p(F_{a},F_{b},\theta;G)]\leq\sum_{H^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}^{\prime}}c_{max,H^{\prime}}p(H^{\prime};G) (8)

where

cm​i​n,H′=minH∈H′⁡𝐄θ∈ΘH​[p⁡(Fa,Fb,θ,H)]c_{min,H^{\prime}}=\min_{H\in H^{\prime}}\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta_{H}}[p(F_{a},F_{b},\theta;H)]

and

cm​a​x,H′=maxH∈H′⁡𝐄θ∈ΘH​[p⁡(Fa,Fb,θ,H)].c_{max,H^{\prime}}=\max_{H\in H^{\prime}}\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta_{H}}[p(F_{a},F_{b},\theta;H)].

In order to keep quantities like 𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩θT​Q​𝐩θ]\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{\theta}^{T}Q\mathbf{p}_{\theta}] non-negative we have to be careful about whether we apply the upper or lower bound given in (8). We can do this and still represent the problem as a semidefinite program, by replacing the matrix QQ with two matrices Q+Q_{+} and Q−Q_{-} such that Q=Q+−Q−Q=Q_{+}-Q_{-} and the entries of Q+Q_{+} and Q−Q_{-} are all non-negative. Consequently 𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩θT​Q​𝐩θ]=𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩θT​Q+​𝐩θ]−𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩θT​Q−​𝐩θ]\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{\theta}^{T}Q\mathbf{p}_{\theta}]=\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{\theta}^{T}Q_{+}\mathbf{p}_{\theta}]-\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{\theta}^{T}Q_{-}\mathbf{p}_{\theta}] and we can ensure non-negativity by applying upper bounds to terms coming from 𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩θT​Q+​𝐩θ]\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{\theta}^{T}Q_{+}\mathbf{p}_{\theta}] and lower bounds to terms coming from 𝐄θ∈Θ​[𝐩θT​Q−​𝐩θ]\mathbf{E}_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbf{p}_{\theta}^{T}Q_{-}\mathbf{p}_{\theta}].

It is unclear whether this method will ever produce any improvements over the partially defined graph version of Razborov’s method. Also it is not apparent what a good choice for the partition ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} is. Nevertheless it may be worth further investigation.

The study of Turán problems in hypercubes is largely motivated by Erdős’ conjecture that πe​(𝒬2)=1/2\pi_{e}(\mathcal{Q}_{2})=1/2. This is perhaps the most interesting question in the area, and still remains open. We have provided improvements on the bounds of various edge and vertex Turán densities but were only able to calculate πv​(R2)\pi_{v}(R_{2}) exactly. Improving the bounds further to get exact results in any of the problems discussed would be of interest. Also any significant improvement of the bound of π⁡(K43)\pi(K_{4}^{3}) would be interesting.
